beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Here are two pizzas, exactly the same size. Which is more: one third of the same pizza, or one eighth of it?

do.text: Which is more: $\frac{1}{3}$ or $\frac{1}{8}$ of the same pizza?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Easy. An eighth! Eight is bigger than three.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That is the trap. In a minute, you will simply see the answer. No measuring needed.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Share the first pizza among three friends. Three equal slices.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Share the second pizza among eight friends. Eight equal slices.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One friend takes one slice from the first pizza: one slice out of three.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That is one third.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now one slice from the second pizza: one slice out of eight.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That is one eighth.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Whoa. The eighth is so thin!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three friends share: big slices. Eight friends share: thin slices. The more people share, the smaller each share.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Slide the thin slice onto the big one.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: It fits inside, with room to spare. One third is more than one eighth.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So a bigger bottom number means a smaller slice!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Yes. More cuts, smaller pieces.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Fractions can be parts of a rectangle too. Here is one strip, the same whole every time. Cut it in two equal pieces and take one: one half.

do.text: One whole, cut into more pieces

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The same whole, cut in three. One third. See how much shorter?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Cut in four. One fourth. Shorter again.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Cut in six. One sixth.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Cut in eight. One eighth. A tiny piece.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Every time the bottom number grows, the single piece shrinks. One eighth fits inside every one of the others.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So with the same top number, fewer cuts wins!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Right. Same count, so the bigger piece wins, and bigger pieces come from fewer cuts.

do.text: Same top number: fewer cuts, bigger pieces, greater fraction

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now two fractions with the same bottom number: two sixths, and five sixths of the same whole.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Both strips are cut into sixths, so every piece is exactly the same size.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Two sixths means two of those pieces. One, two.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Five sixths means five pieces. One, two, three, four, five.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Same size pieces, so five pieces is more than two pieces!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Exactly. Five sixths is more than two sixths. When the bottom numbers match, just count the pieces.

do.text: Same bottom number: more pieces is more

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now the other way around. Three fourths, and three eighths. The top numbers match: three pieces each.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Take three pieces from each. One, two, three.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: But the pieces are not the same size this time.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Right! Fourths are big. Eighths are small. Three big pieces against three small ones.

do.text: Fourths are big, eighths are small

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Look how soon the small ones run out. Three fourths is more than three eighths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Same top number: the smaller bottom number means bigger pieces, so it wins.

do.text: Same top number: fewer cuts, bigger pieces, greater fraction

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now let us write what we found. The sign opens its wide mouth toward the bigger fraction.

do.text: The wide mouth faces the bigger fraction

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Five sixths is greater than two sixths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One third is greater than one eighth.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three eighths is less than three fourths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: And when two fractions are exactly the same, we use the equals sign. Four sixths equals four sixths.

do.text: Exactly the same amount: equals sign

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One more thing, and it matters. Here is a big pizza and a small pizza.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Take one half of each.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Both are one half, so they are equal!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Are they? Slide the small half onto the big half.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Oh. The small half is much smaller!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A half of a small pizza is not a half of a big one. We can only compare fractions of the same whole.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: So there are two ways to compare, and you can see both. First, same size pieces.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Every piece is the same size, so the strip with more pieces is more.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Second, the same count of pieces.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now the pieces are different sizes. Fewer cuts make bigger pieces, so the bigger piece wins.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: And always the same whole. Then eight being bigger than three cannot fool me.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Same pieces? Count them. Same count? Look at the size of a piece.
